messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Daniel Weber was 68, a married psychologist who had spent much of his life helping other people make sense of fear, yet he now found himself arranging his own days around it. The abuse had taken place years earlier with a romantic partner who could turn suddenly humiliating and violent, and what remained of that relationship for Daniel was not a clean narrative but a series of jagged impressions. When he tries to describe it, he cannot make a clear story even to himself; it is more like a set of photographs that flash in his mind, one frame at a time, and sometimes only the raw emotional force returns without any image at all. A glimpse of a bicycle leaning against a wall, being alone with a woman in an enclosed space, or stepping into a crowded, overstimulating room can pull him straight back into that old alarm. In those moments he feels his mind tighten around the need to manage himself: he tries hard to control his emotions, never allows himself to feel or express anger, and has even started avoiding wearing clothing that resembles what he wore during the relationship, as if some accidental resemblance might expose him.  

What Daniel feels at the time of those reminders is not just discomfort but immediate danger. When he passes a bicycle on the street near his office, or finds himself in a conference room with several people talking at once, he begins watching others closely for signs that they might harm him. Crowds leave him especially unsettled, and being alone with women can make his body go rigid with suspicion, as though he is waiting for the first shift in tone or expression that will tell him he is unsafe. These moments do not simply frighten him; they also confirm what he has come to believe. He has become convinced that people are not what they seem, that the world no longer works by any rules he can trust, and that he is somehow inadequate for having missed the danger before. He was once proud of his professional composure, yet now he is ashamed of how easily he is thrown off balance, and that shame deepens his conviction that he should be able to hold himself together better than he does.  

The more he lives inside those beliefs, the more his habits harden. Because he has come to see danger everywhere, he manages himself with increasingly strict discipline, keeping his face controlled and his anger locked away, as if any visible feeling might make him vulnerable again. That same effort to suppress emotion has made the memories less orderly rather than more; when he clamps down on anger and fear, the event returns less as a narrative than as fragments, and those fragments strengthen the sense that what happened was real and still unresolved. The safer he tries to make himself by controlling what he feels, the more those photographic flashes intrude, and the more he notices the world for possible threats. He wakes during the night to check whether he is safe, because darkness feels different to him than daytime, and the night vigilance has become part of his routine. Even in his own home he scans the environment, listening for movement, and that constant checking keeps the old images active.  

Over time, Daniel’s attempts to protect himself have also narrowed where he will go and how he will move through the world. He steers around bicycles, sidesteps crowded spaces when he can, and becomes uneasy in situations where he might be alone with women, all of which makes ordinary errands and social obligations more complicated. In his work as a psychologist, these precautions are harder to hide; he has declined some meetings, felt tense in waiting rooms, and chosen routes and schedules that reduce chance encounters. Yet each avoidance also leaves him with fewer moments of feeling settled, and the less he tolerates the reminders, the more powerful they become when he cannot escape them. The fear is fed by his own vigilance, and the vigilance is fed by the fear. Daniel now finds himself exhausted by the effort of keeping his emotions contained, by the nightly checking, and by the pressure to seem calm while feeling continually on guard. What finally brought him to seek help was the realization that he was living as if danger were everywhere and himself were fundamentally unprotected, and he is now hoping that treatment might help him recover some sense of safety and a more coherent account of what happened, even if he remains afraid that without constant control he will be overwhelmed by what he has tried so hard to keep inside.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly show Daniel's negative appraisals causing or generating the triggering cues/reminders; it shows reminders leading to beliefs, but not beliefs leading to new triggers.
